name: Ronnie Wood
milestone_by_age_26: Was a member of the Jeff Beck Group by age 20, recording two albums (Truth 1968, Beck-Ola 1969), and co-founded Faces by age 22, co-writing the title track of their LP Ooh La La (1973) at age 26.
early_history_summary: Wood grew up in a musical working-class household in Yiewsley, West London, where his father played harmonica and his older brothers were accomplished musicians and graphic artists. He began playing guitar at 14 after his brothers chipped in to buy him an acoustic, and turned professional at 17 with R&B band the Birds in 1964. By 1967 he joined the Jeff Beck Group alongside Rod Stewart, recording two influential albums before departing to form Faces in 1969.
primary_leverage_engine: Early specialization in London R&B scene
family_context_summary: Born into a working-class family of English canal barge operators ('bargees') in Hillingdon; father was a tugboat skipper and harmonica player, mother a factory worker turned housewife. Grew up in a council house.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father played harmonica in a big band and led musical gatherings at home; older brothers Ted and Art were accomplished musicians and graphic designers who bought Ronnie his first guitar and exposed him to London's 1950s music scene.
primary_early_advantage_tags: London 1960s R&B scene, musical family, sibling collaboration, British blues boom
evidence_summary: Wood grew up in a working-class bargee family in West London but was immersed in music from birth through his father's harmonica playing and his older brothers' musical and artistic careers. His brothers bought him his first guitar and created a hip 1950s music scene in the family's council house. London in the 1960s was the epicenter of the British R&B and rock explosion, giving Wood direct access to the most vibrant music ecosystem of the era. He turned professional at 17 and within three years was recording with Jeff Beck and Rod Stewart, leveraging complementary partnerships and the structural wave of British rock.
starting_point: Born to a working-class family of English canal barge operators in Hillingdon, London; father was a tugboat skipper and harmonica player, mother a former factory worker.
current_position: Member of the Rolling Stones since 1975; still actively touring and recording at age 78; estimated net worth ~$200 million.

trajectory.event: Began professional music career as lead guitarist with R&B band the Birds in London.
Joined the Jeff Beck Group as guitarist and bassist, recording Truth (1968) and Beck-Ola (1969) with Rod Stewart.
Co-founded Faces with Rod Stewart and former Small Faces members, becoming the band's lead guitarist.
Co-wrote and sang the title track of Faces' final LP Ooh La La.
Joined the Rolling Stones as replacement for Mick Taylor, beginning a 50-year tenure with the band.
Released first solo album I've Got My Own Album to Do, featuring contributions from Keith Richards and George Harrison.
Continued touring and recording with the Rolling Stones, including the Hackney Diamonds album cycle.

name: Slavko Vinčić
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Vinčić began refereeing at age 20 (1999) but did not become a Slovenian top-flight referee until 2007 (age 28) or receive a FIFA badge until 2010 (age 31). His major appointments (Europa League final 2022, Champions League final 2024, World Cup final 2026) all came well after 26.
early_history_summary: Vinčić grew up in Maribor, Slovenia, where his first love was basketball. He left high school at 18 to study telecommunications engineering but felt something was missing. At age 20, encouraged by his uncle who was an assistant referee, he took up refereeing and gradually progressed through Slovenian football levels.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond mention that his uncle was an assistant referee who encouraged him to try refereeing.
parent_family_domain_summary: His uncle was an assistant referee, which directly influenced his entry into refereeing at age 20.
evidence_summary: Vinčić began refereeing at age 20 after his uncle encouraged him, having previously focused on basketball and telecommunications engineering studies. He progressed slowly through Slovenian football refereeing levels, not reaching the top flight until age 28 and the FIFA international list until age 31. All his major career achievements came well after age 26.

name: Arthur B. McDonald
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. McDonald earned his BSc (1964, age 21) and MSc (1965, age 22) from Dalhousie, then began PhD studies at Caltech. His PhD was completed around 1969-70 at age 27. His Nobel Prize-winning neutrino research came decades later at the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory.
early_history_summary: McDonald grew up in Sydney, Nova Scotia, and was inspired by a high school math teacher to pursue science. He studied physics at Dalhousie University, earning his BSc and MSc, then moved to Caltech for doctoral work under Charles Barnes in the Kellogg Radiation Laboratory. His academic path was standard for a physicist, with no notable independent milestone before age 27.
family_context_summary: Grew up in a tight-knit family in the small Nova Scotia city of Sydney. No evidence of unusual financial resources or scientific family background.
evidence_summary: McDonald followed a standard academic path through Dalhousie (BSc, MSc) and Caltech (PhD), completing his doctorate around age 27. His Nobel Prize-winning work on neutrino oscillations at the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory came decades later. No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found beyond standard educational progression.

name: Serhiy Shaptala
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Shaptala entered military school in 1990 (age 17), graduated around 1994 (age 21), and served as a junior officer (platoon commander) through his mid-twenties. His major achievements — Hero of Ukraine (2015), Chief of General Staff (2021) — all came well after age 26.
early_history_summary: Shaptala was born in Kostiantynivka, Cherkasy Oblast, and entered the Kyiv Higher Combined Arms Command School in 1990, which was later reorganized into the Odessa Institute of Land Forces. After graduating around 1994, he served as a platoon commander in the 51st Mechanized Division in Volodymyr-Volynskyi, working his way through standard military career progression.
evidence_summary: Shaptala followed a standard military career path, entering military school at 17 and graduating as a platoon commander around age 21. By age 26 he was a junior officer with no notable independent milestone. His significant achievements — commanding the 128th Brigade at Debaltseve, receiving Hero of Ukraine, and becoming Chief of the General Staff — all came after age 40.

name: Tatsuya Shiji
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1959 Emperor's Cup with Kwangaku Club at age 21, and debuted and scored for the Japan national team on May 28, 1961 at age 22 — both material milestones before age 26.
early_history_summary: Shiji was born in Aichi Prefecture and attended Atsuta High School before enrolling at Kwansei Gakuin University in 1958. As a university student, he played for the Kwangaku Club (composed of university players and graduates) and won the prestigious Emperor's Cup in 1959. He debuted for the Japan national team in 1961, scoring against Malaya, and graduated in 1962 to join Toyota Motors.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Born in Aichi Prefecture, Japan.
primary_early_advantage_tags: university football, Emperor's Cup, Japan national team
evidence_summary: Shiji's early career was built around the university football pipeline in Japan: he attended Kwansei Gakuin University, where the Kwangaku Club provided a competitive platform that won the 1959 Emperor's Cup. His national team debut at age 22 with a goal against Malaya was a material milestone. Family background and early training details are not documented in reviewed sources, limiting the ability to assess early advantages.
starting_point: Born in Aichi Prefecture, Japan; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Former football player and manager; served as head of the Aichi Prefecture Football Association after managing Toyota Motors (1965-1974). Now retired at age 87.

trajectory.event: Won the Emperor's Cup with Kwangaku Club as a Kwansei Gakuin University student.
Debuted and scored for the Japan national team against Malaya on May 28.
Graduated from Kwansei Gakuin University and joined Toyota Motors football club.
Became manager of Toyota Motors, launching a decade-long coaching career.
Led Toyota Motors to the Japan Soccer League Division 2 championship.
Promoted Toyota Motors to JSL Division 1 as manager.

name: Ivan Reitman
milestone_by_age_26: Produced the feature film Columbus of Sex (1969) at age 23 — which was banned by the Ontario Board of Censors and resulted in an obscenity conviction — and his first 35mm feature Foxy Lady (1971) at age 25, establishing himself as a commercially releasing film producer before age 26.
early_history_summary: Reitman was born in Czechoslovakia to Holocaust survivor parents who fled to Canada as refugees when he was four. At McMaster University, he headed the McMaster Film Board and made a short film, Orientation, which he sold to CBC and 20th Century Fox. He produced his first feature, Columbus of Sex, in 1969, followed by Foxy Lady (1971) and Cannibal Girls (1973), building a career in low-budget independent filmmaking before his major breakthrough with Animal House (1978).
family_context_summary: Born to Hungarian Jewish parents in Komárno, Czechoslovakia; mother survived Auschwitz, father was an underground resistance fighter. Family arrived in Canada as penniless refugees in 1950 and settled in Toronto, where parents eventually owned a small chain of dry cleaners and a car wash.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were not in the film industry; they were working-class immigrants who built a small dry-cleaning business. No domain advantage transferred.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Holocaust survivor parents, refugee immigrant, McMaster Film Board, Dan Goldberg collaboration, Canadian film scene
evidence_summary: Reitman's early career was shaped by extreme adversity: his parents were Holocaust survivors who fled to Canada as penniless refugees. He leveraged access to film equipment through McMaster University's Film Board and a National Film Board summer course, and built a complementary partnership with producer Dan Goldberg. His determination was evident in re-cutting and selling his banned film Columbus of Sex to an American distributor for profit. The Canadian film industry's development in the late 1960s provided a modest structural wave, but his early milestones were driven primarily by entrepreneurial hustle rather than inherited advantages.
starting_point: Born to Hungarian Jewish Holocaust survivor parents in Komárno, Czechoslovakia; family fled as penniless refugees to Toronto, Canada in 1950, where parents built a small dry-cleaning business.
current_position: Died February 12, 2022 at age 75 in Montecito, California; final role was producer of Ghostbusters: Afterlife (2021). Owner of The Montecito Picture Company, founded 1998.

trajectory.event: Produced feature film Columbus of Sex at McMaster University; film was banned by Ontario censors and Reitman was convicted of obscenity.
Produced his first 35mm feature film Foxy Lady, establishing himself as a commercial film producer.
Directed horror comedy Cannibal Girls, which he sold profitably to American International Pictures at Cannes.
Produced National Lampoon's Animal House, one of the highest-grossing comedies of all time and his major breakthrough.
Directed Meatballs, Bill Murray's first lead film role and one of the highest-grossing Canadian features ever.
Directed Ghostbusters, one of the most successful comedies in cinema history and a major cultural phenomenon.
Founded The Montecito Picture Company production company.
Died on February 12 in Montecito, California; final producer credit on Ghostbusters: Afterlife (2021).

name: François Englert
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Englert earned his electrical-mechanical engineering degree in 1955 (age 23) and Physics Masters in 1958 (age 26). His PhD was completed in 1959 at age 27. His Nobel Prize-winning work on the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism was published in 1964 at age 32.
early_history_summary: Englert was born in Etterbeek, Belgium to a Jewish family. During the German occupation, he concealed his Jewish roots and hid in orphanages. He studied electrical-mechanical engineering at the Université Libre de Bruxelles, graduating in 1955, then pursued physics, earning his Masters in 1958 and PhD in 1959. His groundbreaking work on spontaneous symmetry breaking came years later at Cornell University and ULB.
family_context_summary: Born to a Jewish family in Etterbeek, Belgium. During WWII, he concealed his Jewish identity and hid at different orphanages to survive the German occupation.
evidence_summary: Englert followed a standard academic path through ULB (engineering degree, physics Masters, PhD) by his mid-twenties. His Nobel Prize-winning work on the Higgs mechanism was published in 1964 at age 32, well after age 26. No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found beyond standard educational degrees.

name: Robert Huber
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Huber earned his chemistry diploma in 1960 (age 23) and completed his PhD thesis on crystal structure of a diazo compound in 1963 (age 26). His Nobel Prize-winning work on photosynthetic reaction centers came in the 1980s. The ecdysone finding during his diploma work was a scientific result but part of standard academic training, not an independently notable milestone.
early_history_summary: Huber was born in Munich to a bank cashier father and housewife mother. He studied chemistry at the Technische Hochschule München, receiving his diploma in 1960. He joined crystallographer W. Hoppe's laboratory and found the molecular weight and steroid nature of ecdysone during his diploma work. His PhD thesis was completed in 1963 on the crystal structure of a diazo compound.
family_context_summary: Born in Munich as the first child of Sebastian Huber, a bank cashier, and Helene Huber, a housewife. The family struggled during the war years. Huber attended the Humanistische Karls-Gymnasium with strong Latin and Greek instruction.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father was a bank cashier with no apparent scientific background.
evidence_summary: Huber followed a standard academic path through the Technische Hochschule München (diploma 1960, PhD 1963), completing his doctorate at approximately age 26. While his diploma work on ecdysone yielded a meaningful scientific finding, it was part of standard academic training rather than an independently notable milestone. His Nobel Prize-winning crystallography work came decades later at the Max Planck Institute.

name: Rigoberta Menchú
milestone_by_age_26: Published the testimonial biography I, Rigoberta Menchú in 1983 at age 24, which attracted considerable international attention to indigenous rights in Guatemala. She was also a prominent organizer in the Committee of the Peasant Union (CUC) from 1979, led a major farm workers' strike in 1980, and was active in large demonstrations in 1981 — all before age 26.
early_history_summary: Menchú was born to a poor K'iche' Maya peasant family in Laj Chimel, Guatemala, and worked on plantations from age eight. She became involved in social reform through the Catholic Church as a teenager and joined the CUC in 1979 at age 20. After her father was killed in the 1980 Spanish Embassy storming and her mother was tortured and murdered, she became increasingly prominent as an activist, organizing strikes and demonstrations before fleeing to Mexico in 1981. Her testimonial biography, published in 1983, brought international fame.
family_context_summary: Born to a poor K'iche' Maya indigenous peasant family in rural Guatemala. Father Vicente was a day laborer and community activist; mother Juana was a midwife and traditional healer. Multiple family members were killed by the military during the Guatemalan Civil War.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a prominent activist for indigenous farmers' rights who joined the Committee of the Peasant Union (CUC); mother was a traditional midwife and healer serving 18 villages. Both parents were Catholic lay leaders who involved their children in pastoral and activist activities.
primary_early_advantage_tags: indigenous poverty, family activism, Catholic Church, civil war, CUC organizing, testimonial biography
evidence_summary: Menchú's early trajectory was defined by extreme adversity and direct lived experience of indigenous oppression in Guatemala. Her father was a community activist who mentored her in organizing through the CUC, and the Catholic Church provided a platform for her early social reform work. The Guatemalan Civil War and the murder of her father, mother, and brother by security forces catalyzed her international activism. Her 1983 testimonial biography I, Rigoberta Menchú became a vehicle for global distribution of her cause, making her an internationally recognized figure by age 24.
starting_point: Born to a poor K'iche' Maya indigenous peasant family in Laj Chimel, a remote village in the Guatemalan highlands; father was a day laborer and community activist, mother a midwife and traditional healer.
current_position: Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1992); UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador; founder of indigenous political party Winaq; ran for president of Guatemala in 2007 and 2011; continues activism for indigenous rights at age 67.

trajectory.event: Joined the Committee of the Peasant Union (CUC), following her father's activist legacy.
Figured prominently in a CUC-organized strike for better conditions for farm workers on the Pacific coast; father killed in Spanish Embassy storming.
Active in large demonstrations in Guatemala City on May 1; forced into hiding and then fled to Mexico.
Published testimonial biography I, Rigoberta Menchú with Elisabeth Burgos Debray, gaining international attention.
Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle for social justice and indigenous rights.
Named UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador; peace agreement signed in Guatemala with Norway as intermediary.
Founded Winaq, Guatemala's first indigenous political party, and ran for president.

name: Felipe Muñoz
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Olympic gold medal in the 200m breaststroke at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics at age 17 — Mexico's first-ever Olympic swimming gold medal and a landmark moment in Mexican Olympic history.
early_history_summary: Muñoz was born in Mexico City and began swimming at age 12 at Club Vanguardia, initially preferring basketball. He was discovered by coach Nelson Vargas, who provided daily training from 5am at IMSS facilities. By 1966, he was selected for the Mexican national team under American coach Ronald Johnson. At 17, he won a surprise Olympic gold in the 200m breaststroke at the 1968 Mexico City Games, coming from behind in one of the most emotional races in Olympic history.
family_context_summary: Born in Mexico City to a family of modest means; parents separated when he was young, causing financial hardship. Family lived in the Colonia Roma area. Mother worked in the administrative department of a bus company. Of Greek descent on his mother's side.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental involvement in swimming or sports.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Mexico 1968 Olympics, IMSS training facilities, Nelson Vargas coaching, Ronald Johnson national team, altitude advantage
evidence_summary: Muñoz benefited from Mexico hosting the 1968 Olympics, which created a national performance pipeline with dedicated facilities and foreign coaching expertise. His coach Nelson Vargas provided sustained, individualized training from age 12, picking him up daily at 5am. The IMSS swimming program and national team selection under American coach Ronald Johnson concentrated opportunity. Despite family financial hardship and parents' separation, the structural advantage of a home Olympics combined with dedicated coaching enabled his surprise gold medal at age 17.
starting_point: Born in Mexico City to a family of modest means; parents separated during his childhood, causing financial hardship. Mother worked at a bus company administrative department.
current_position: President of the Mexican Olympic Committee since 2008; former Deputy in the Mexican Congress; graduate of the University of Texas. Resides in Mexico City at age 74.

trajectory.event: Won Olympic gold medal in the 200m breaststroke at the Mexico City Olympics, Mexico's first-ever swimming gold.
Won silver in 200m breaststroke and bronze in 200m IM at the Pan American Games in Cali.
Served as Mexico's flagbearer at the Munich Olympics; placed fifth in the 200m breaststroke final.
Graduated with a degree in Communication and Publicity from the University of Texas.
Became head of the Mexican Sports Confederation (CODEME), serving until 2001.
Became President of the Mexican Olympic Committee.

name: Mariss Jansons
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Jansons was still a student at the Leningrad Conservatory at age 26. His major career milestones — winning second prize at the Karajan Conducting Competition (1971, age 28), becoming Mravinsky's assistant at the Leningrad Philharmonic (1971-72, age 28-29), and being appointed Music Director of the Oslo Philharmonic (1979, age 36) — all came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Jansons was born in Riga, Latvia, the son of conductor Arvīds Jansons. He moved to Leningrad in 1956 at age 13 when his father became assistant conductor to Mravinsky at the Leningrad Philharmonic. He studied conducting at the Leningrad Conservatory under Nikolai Rabinovich. In 1968, Herbert von Karajan singled him out from young conductors, but Soviet authorities blocked the resulting opportunities. His career breakthroughs came after age 28.
family_context_summary: Born in Riga to conductor Arvīds Jansons and soprano Iraida Jansons. His mother was Jewish; her father and brother were murdered by the Nazis. The family moved to Leningrad in 1956 when his father was appointed assistant conductor to Mravinsky at the Leningrad Philharmonic.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was conductor of the Riga Opera and later assistant conductor at the Leningrad Philharmonic under Mravinsky. Mother was a principal soprano. This provided direct immersion in the world of classical music from birth.
evidence_summary: Despite being the son of a prominent conductor and growing up immersed in the Leningrad Philharmonic ecosystem, Jansons was still a conservatory student at age 26 with no material independently verifiable milestone. His career was hindered by Soviet authorities who blocked opportunities offered by Karajan. His major appointments — assistant conductor at the Leningrad Philharmonic (1971), Music Director of the Oslo Philharmonic (1979) — all came after age 28.

name: Sonia Rykiel
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Rykiel was working as a window dresser at a Parisian textile store from age 17 (1948) and married Sam Rykiel in 1953. Her design breakthrough — the Poor Boy Sweater — came in 1962 at age 32, and her first boutique opened in 1968 at age 38. No material design or fashion milestone occurred by age 26.
early_history_summary: Rykiel was born Sonia Flis to Jewish parents in Neuilly-sur-Seine, France. Her father was a Romanian watchmaker and her mother was Polish. She worked as a window dresser at the Grande Maison de Blanc in Paris from age 17. She married Sam Rykiel, owner of a Paris boutique, in 1953. Her fashion career began only in 1962 when she designed maternity clothes during her pregnancy, leading to the Poor Boy Sweater.
family_context_summary: Born to Jewish parents in Neuilly-sur-Seine; father was a Romanian watchmaker, mother was Polish. Eldest of five sisters. Married Sam Rykiel, owner of a Paris boutique, in 1953 at age 23.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father was a watchmaker with no apparent fashion industry connection.
evidence_summary: Rykiel was working as a window dresser in Paris from age 17 and married a boutique owner at 23, but her fashion design career did not begin until 1962 at age 32 when she created the Poor Boy Sweater during her pregnancy. Her first boutique opened in 1968 at age 38. No material milestone in fashion design or any other domain occurred by age 26.
